**Diagnosis:** Chronic venous ulcer (gaiter-area), mixed venous-arterial etiology, secondary to post-thrombotic syndrome.  
**Key supporting evidence:**

[THOUGHT]  
This case presents a chronic, non-healing gaiter-area ulcer in the context of long-standing bilateral leg edema and a prior right DVT—strongly implicating post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS) as the primary venous pathophysiology. Duplex ultrasonography objectively confirms both venous reflux *and* obstruction across superficial and deep systems on the affected side—fulfilling imaging criteria for PTS. The presence of palpable (though diminished) distal pulses, absence of ischemic skin changes (e.g., hair loss, atrophy, rest pain, tissue necrosis), and normal systemic markers (WBC, Hb, platelets) argue against critical limb ischemia or active infection. The mixed venous-arterial label is appropriate: arterial compromise is mild and likely functional (edema-induced pulse dampening, perifibrotic compression), not structural—consistent with “venous claudication” or pseudo-arterial insufficiency. Family history of similar venous disease supports underlying heritable venous wall/valvular pathology (e.g., FOXC2, SOX18 variants), further reinforcing chronic venous etiology over alternative causes. No features suggest vasculitis, neuropathic ulceration, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. The diagnosis is high-certainty because all major diagnostic criteria for chronic venous ulcer with PTS are met *and* key mimics are robustly excluded by objective data.

- 6-month non-healing ulcer located in the gaiter area (classic location for venous ulcers)  
- 10+ years of chronic bilateral leg edema (chronic venous hypertension)  
- Prior right DVT 5 years ago (established cause of post-thrombotic syndrome)  
- Duplex ultrasonography shows venous reflux + obstruction in both superficial and deep venous systems of the right leg (definitive objective evidence of PTS)  
- Diminished but palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses (mild arterial compromise, consistent with functional impairment rather than critical stenosis)  
- Negative wound culture (excludes active infection as driver of non-healing)  
- Normal WBC, hemoglobin, and platelets (excludes systemic inflammation, anemia of chronic disease, or thrombocytopenia-related healing impairment)  
- Absence of diabetes, neuropathy, trauma history, malignancy risk factors, or autoimmune features (rules out major alternative ulcer etiologies)  
- Positive family history of venous disease in mother and brother (supports heritable venous insufficiency)

[GAPS]

- No assessment of venous filling time, calf pump ejection fraction, or perforator incompetence severity on duplex (not essential for diagnosis but relevant for staging and management)  
- No skin biopsy or histopathology — though not indicated given classic presentation and absence of atypical features (e.g., rolled borders, induration, rapid growth), it would definitively exclude malignancy or vasculitis if clinical doubt arose  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Chronic venous ulcer secondary to post-thrombotic syndrome

The diagnosis is high-certainty because all major diagnostic criteria for chronic venous ulcer with PTS are met *and* key mimics are robustly excluded by objective data.

[EVIDENCE]  
- 6-month non-healing ulcer located in the gaiter area (classic location for venous ulcers)  
- 10+ years of chronic bilateral leg edema (chronic venous hypertension)  
- Prior right DVT 5 years ago (established cause of post-thrombotic syndrome)  
- Duplex ultrasonography shows venous reflux + obstruction in both superficial and deep venous systems of the right leg (definitive objective evidence of PTS)  
- Diminished but palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses (mild arterial compromise, consistent with functional impairment rather than critical stenosis)  
- Negative wound culture (excludes active infection as driver of non-healing)  
- Normal WBC, hemoglobin, and platelets (excludes systemic inflammation, anemia of chronic disease, or thrombocytopenia-related healing impairment)  
- Absence of diabetes, neuropathy, trauma history, malignancy risk factors, or autoimmune features (rules out major alternative ulcer etiologies)  
- Positive family history of venous disease in mother and brother (supports heritable venous insufficiency)

[GAPS]  
- Ankle-brachial index (ABI) not reported — required to quantify arterial sufficiency before initiating high-compression therapy  
- No assessment of venous filling time, calf pump ejection fraction, or perforator incompetence severity on duplex (not essential for diagnosis but relevant for staging and management)  
- No skin biopsy or histopathology — though not indicated given classic presentation and absence of atypical features (e.g., rolled borders, induration, rapid growth), it would definitively exclude malignancy or vasculitis if clinical doubt arose  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Chronic venous ulcer secondary to post-thrombotic syndrome
